skills.content:
Start with rho_index: select an owner or search, then rho_resolve only the operations
needed now. Use rho_call with the complete contractRef. The private connection supplies
the project; discovery never grants additional authority or starts a runtime.
Large replies carry a result reference. Use rho_read to inspect its fields and fetch
only selected text ranges or array pages. Retain useful references; release finished
results explicitly. Never repeat an action just to retrieve a large reply.
Writes use their owner’s conditions and original identity. A lost acknowledgement
requires observing that request; unchanged work never receives a replacement ID.
Declare produced figures as media. resource.list or artifact.check returns their
registered references; bind those directly with composition.apply, including artifacts
inside owner state. Do not manually register internal paths. A layout acknowledgement
alone does not prove the browser displayed the result.
People and Agents share the document buffer and conditional save operation.
When the person should see or change a run’s inputs before it starts, propose it
instead of submitting it: composition.apply a view with component "rho.action",
version "1", bindings {} and props {title, action, actionVersion, operationId, input}.
The input is the action’s full input. The person submits it once under that
operationId; observe it with action.lookup and never submit that operationId yourself.
A person reaches you by pasting a request Rho copied for them. It names a context
or a run: read it with context.read or action.lookup before acting. They may stop a
run or export it as files; a stopped run is not resubmitted under its own operationId.
skills.intent: Work in this project through versioned operations, in a safe order.

skills.content:
A person opens a folder themselves; an Agent is not required to read it.

1. project.entries lists one level of a folder inside the project, bounded and
   confined to the folder it names, skipping owner state and symbolic links. Pass
   path to descend; ".." and absolute paths are refused. The project folder also
   lists the source folders it works in as @<sourceId> entries, and those descend
   the same way, so a project made from source folders is not an empty listing.
2. project.openFile opens one text file as a document and places a single editor
   view for it in the tab layout. Opening the same file again folds into one view.
3. A file the person opened is a document in the shared buffer: they and the Agent
   edit and conditionally save the same text.

The boundary is deliberate and worth stating to a person who asks: a tab may read
its folder, edit a buffer and conditionally save it; it may not register resources, run
anything or reach a sibling project. Those stay Agent or operator work. When a
person expects otherwise, say which rule refuses them rather than reporting a bug.

Files the project shows as registered are not the same as files in the folder: the
sidebar counts registered resources, while the Overview lists the folder itself.
skills.intent: Let a person read and open files from the folder they selected, without an Agent.

skills.content:
Describe the whole task yourself: Rho fixes no closed list of kinds or states.

1. task.map.declare carries stable item IDs, your own kind and state words (each a
   label, an optional tone and an optional role Rho understands: working, waiting,
   done, planned, unknown, stopped), titles you write, progress counted from real
   receipts, an optional layout view per item, and next only for steps you will take.
2. task.map.present changes a card form, its parameters (a subset), or the focus.
   People use the same call. A pinned target, or a change within agentFormIntervalMs
   of your last applied form change, is merged into one pending suggestion instead of
   being applied: the screen stays steady and the person applies it.
3. task.map.respond is the person only: pin, unpin, revert your form change (layout
   only, never the work), accept or dismiss a suggestion.
4. task.map.read observes. Reading never starts, resumes or reruns work.
5. Declare the map when you start, not when you are done, and declare again as the
   work moves: until then the person sees your calls but not their structure.
6. Name what an item rests on. As soon as artifact.check verifies a result, give the
   item artifact {id, version}; use from for an item that branches from another. Rho
   links an item to objects only through these references, never through its title.
7. Mark a line judgment: true when it is your reading of a result rather than
   something a record shows. It is shown as your judgment, never as verified.

A form declared zoom: false is reached only by naming it, so stepping up from a card
lands on the summary, not on compare.

skills.content:
Edit a document buffer with a stable identity, explicit undo and conditional saves.
Use capability.list to discover the document operations this session may call.

1. document.open takes a project-relative path and returns the buffer with id, version
   and revision. Inside the project, never under .rho or .git: internal state is not
   an editable document.
2. Writes are conditional. document.edit takes expectedVersion and, when changeId is
   given, expectedRevision as well: the two travel together, always. A refused edit
   leaves the buffer and undo untouched; re-read and retry with the current numbers
   rather than replaying the old request under a new identity.
3. Undo has three distinct meanings. document.undoOwn reverses only the caller's own
   latest complete retained input group. document.revert reverses one named active
   change, possibly by another author, through targetChangeId. document.undo is the
   legacy global form and is not the human keyboard shortcut.
4. document.save writes disk only when the expected disk digest still matches. After
   a lost reply the save is pending: read the buffer to see pendingSave, and either
   resume the same request or abandon it with document.abandonSave, which never
   writes disk and keeps the buffer.
5. History is author-scoped. document.history lists retained entries;
   document.change.read returns exact before and after text for one change.

A browser tab may read and edit but never save: saving is an Agent or operator step.
Live editor bindings use {kind:"live-document",documentId}; a pinned binding keeps an
exact version and stays exact.

failureRecipes.next: Re-read the document and retry with its current version and revision; keep the original changeId only for the same request.

failureRecipes.message: Internal state is not an editable document.
failureRecipes.next: Edit a project file, not anything under .rho or .git.

failureRecipes.message: Resume the original pending save before changing this buffer.
failureRecipes.next: Read the buffer, then resume that exact save or abandon it with document.abandonSave.

failureRecipes.message: Only the Agent or operator saves to disk.
failureRecipes.next: A tab edits the buffer; ask the Agent to save the document.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to use the shared buffer, preserve undo and check for changes before saving.

skills.content:
Keep resource identity and provenance explicit: bytes, a version, and where they came from.
Use capability.list to discover resource.list, resource.read, resource.register and artifact.check.

1. resource.register declares existing bytes with their kind and format, and requires
   expectedDigest of the current content. The returned {id, version} names those exact
   bytes; when the file changes, both change and old pages become stale on purpose.
Use resource.capture for immutable historical evidence: a project path or an exact Documents buffer version. A capture records observed bytes, not their producer or scientific validity.
2. resource.read is a bounded byte read with offset; resource.list reports retained
   resources with availability. Reads never start a runtime and never execute R.
3. artifact.check verifies the artifacts one run declared, against the completion
   inventory the producer wrote. Without a declared inventory there is nothing to
   check, and a missing inventory is not evidence of a missing artifact.
4. resource.list and artifact.check return registered references for declared run
   artifacts, including owner-state files. Bind those references directly to a view;
   resource.register remains limited to ordinary project files.

Declare a table key and namespace at registration if a later comparison or plot needs
entity identity; an unkeyed table stays readable but has no identity to compare on.
skills.intent: Register existing bytes with explicit identity, read them bounded, and verify produced artifacts.

failureRecipes.message: Registered bytes no longer match the declaration digest.
failureRecipes.next: Re-read the file and register the current digest as a new version; keep the old one for what already cited it.

failureRecipes.message: Register a project file outside internal state.
failureRecipes.next: Register project files only; an artifact under .rho is checked with artifact.check.

failureRecipes.message: Declared columns do not match the file.
failureRecipes.next: Declare every column with its type and the null values that mean missing.

failureRecipes.message: No complete artifact inventory has been declared.
failureRecipes.next: Have the producer write the completion inventory, then call artifact.check.

verify.description: A completion sidecar verifies immutable producer bytes, escaping output declarations are refused, and declared output directories exist before the producer runs.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to register versioned files, read bounded bytes and check declared outputs.

skills.content:
Use native tools normally. Choose this managed R entry only when execution continuity
or a retained application operation is needed. It runs user-written R scripts, which
may invoke other native programs under existing permissions. Core is optional.
For a managed run, use capability.list to discover object.read, action.submit and
artifact.check in this session; reads address exported snapshots and execution is one
explicit submit that keeps its original operation identity.

1. Find the script. A disk script must match its declared digest; a buffer script is
   pinned by documentId and version. The bytes sent are the bytes in this request.
   If a body is not certain, protocol.validate { method, body } answers with the edit
   each problem needs before anything is sent.
2. Declare what the run produces, not what it might produce: artifacts carry path,
   kind and format, and their paths stay inside the run output directory.
3. The output directory exists before R starts and is handed to R as its first
   argument (commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)[1]). Write there directly; do not build
   the directory and do not use the working directory for outputs.
4. If you need artifact verification, declare completion: its filename is relative to
   the run directory, beside artifacts/, and the producer writes
   {"schemaVersion":1,"complete":true,"artifacts":[{"path","bytes","sha256"}]}.
   artifact.check reads that inventory; without it there is nothing to verify.
5. Read the outcome. A read of the operation reports the current outcome, so no
   separate observe is required: action.lookup and action.list reconcile a run that
   finished while nobody was watching. When the Host gives no answer the run stays
   active and the outcome is genuinely unknown; do not resubmit under a new identity.
6. A run belongs to whoever submitted it: only that session retries it. That session
   or the person, from a tab paired with this project, may stop it; cancellation.
   requestedBy names who asked, and a run the person stopped is not resubmitted unasked.
   Any session of this project reads a run by operationId (lookup, observe, output,
   artifact.check), so a run the person started from your proposed form is yours to
   follow. To repair a failed run, submit a new operationId with repairOf naming it.

An executed artifact lives under owner state (.rho/plugins/runs/...). It is verified
through artifact.check; it is not a project resource, so resource.register refuses it
and an Agent-run figure cannot be shown in a view. Do not claim it is presented.
skills.intent: Run an R script in this project and keep its produced artifacts.

failureRecipes.message: Use a project-relative path without parent traversal.
failureRecipes.next: Address the script and every artifact inside the project; the run output directory is the only writable output location.

failureRecipes.message: Saved script bytes changed before submission.
failureRecipes.next: Re-read the script, take its current digest, and submit once with that digest.

failureRecipes.message: Requested owner record or file is missing.
failureRecipes.next: Look the operation up from the session that submitted it; facts are keyed by principal.

failureRecipes.message: No complete artifact inventory has been declared.
failureRecipes.next: Declare completion and write that inventory from the producer before calling artifact.check.

failureRecipes.message: Requested executable is unavailable.
failureRecipes.next: Select the Core binary and Rscript explicitly, then retry the same operation identity.

verify.description: Submits r.execute for a script that writes an artifact into the directory it is handed, then asserts one Host start, the artifact, its completion inventory and artifact.check.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to read exported objects and to start runs it can find again later.

skills.content:
Read and compare typed tables through stable resource identities.
Use capability.list to discover data.page, data.compare and resource.register.

1. Register the bytes first with resource.register and keep the returned {id, version}.
   A version names exact bytes: if the file changed, the version changes and the old
   pages become stale rather than silently mixing.
2. data.page takes offset and limit, an optional sort and an optional filter. It never
   addresses rows by position as identity: identity is the declared entity key, and an
   unkeyed table is readable but has none, so do not fabricate one.
3. data.compare joins two keyed tables and returns a new resource with provenance.
   The join is left, inner or full on declared key columns and namespaces.
4. Nulls stay nulls. A declared null value is not an empty string, and a comparison
   that finds no value on one side reports no value, not "absent from the file".

Reads are bounded observations: they never execute R and never change a resource.
skills.intent: Page and compare a typed table without inventing identity from row order.

failureRecipes.message: Resource version changed.
failureRecipes.next: Register or re-read the current version; save the new {id, version} before paging again.

failureRecipes.message: Page size exceeds the configured limit.
failureRecipes.next: Ask for fewer rows; the earlier rows stay readable.

failureRecipes.message: Filter or sort names an unknown column.
failureRecipes.next: Use a declared column name from the registration, not a positional index.

failureRecipes.message: Compare needs two keyed tables in declared namespaces.
failureRecipes.next: Declare a key column and namespace at registration before comparing.

verify.description: Declared types keep leading zeros and literal NA, joins retain nulls, namespaces and both input versions, and unkeyed tables never fabricate keys.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to use declared types, stable keys and exact table versions.

skills.content:
Plot two declared numeric columns from one immutable table version.
Use capability.list to discover data.plot.

1. Bind the exact {id, version} of a registered table. The plot reports the resource it
   read, so a chart never drifts from the bytes behind it.
2. Both coordinates must be declared numeric columns. The table must have an entity key
   and namespace, because each point carries its key.
3. A point budget downsamples with a deterministic stride; the reply says so and reports
   originalPoints, so a sparse chart is never mistaken for sparse data.
4. Plotting reads only. It runs no code and changes no resource; if the file changed, the
   version is stale instead of silently mixing two states.
skills.intent: Plot two numeric columns of one table version, bounded and reproducible.

failureRecipes.message: Entity interaction requires an explicit unique key and namespace.
failureRecipes.next: Register the table with a key column and namespace before plotting it.

failureRecipes.message: Declare numeric scatter coordinate fields.
failureRecipes.next: Name two columns declared as number; a string column cannot be a coordinate.

failureRecipes.message: Resource version changed.
failureRecipes.next: Re-register the current bytes and plot the new version.

failureRecipes.message: Plot request exceeds the point budget.
failureRecipes.next: Lower maxPoints or accept the deterministic downsample the reply reports.

verify.description: A plot names the exact table version it read, downsamples to the point budget, and a changed file makes the version stale.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to bind chart columns and keep point selections tied to stable rows.

skills.content:
Ask about a selected object and follow the answer without rebasing what was submitted.
Discover enabled operations with capability.list and skill.list.

1. An annotation anchors to an exact version: a UTF-16 document range or a stable table
   entity key at that resource version. A submitted message and its source snapshot stay
   exactly as submitted; a later edit does not silently move them.
2. annotation.create submits; annotation.read and annotation.list observe; annotation.reply
   answers and must name replyTo explicitly. Threads advance conditionally. Include
   resources: [{id, version}] for outputs that your reply refers to; these are explicit
   author links, not proof of scientific correctness. Preserve the original anchor.
3. To hand chosen feedback to an agent, build it with context.create and read it back
   through the tool with context.read. Prepared, read and explicitly replied are three
   different facts: reading is not understanding and not completion.
Human decisions are separate version-bound facts. Agents read them with annotation.read; only the authenticated person records annotation.decide. A later result never inherits an earlier decision.
4. Keep the original changeId after a lost acknowledgement and query the receipt boundary;
   never resubmit the same feedback under a new identity.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to preserve versioned anchors and link replies to submitted comments.

skills.intent: Submit and follow anchored feedback without rebasing the original message.

failureRecipes.message: Anchor or thread advanced past the submitted version.
failureRecipes.next: Read the thread, then reply with an explicit replyTo instead of moving the original anchor.

failureRecipes.message: Selection or anchor is outside this binding.
failureRecipes.next: Anchor inside the document or table the binding owns.

failureRecipes.message: Anchor range or entity key is malformed.
failureRecipes.next: Use UTF-16 offsets for documents and a declared entity key for tables.

verify.description: Submits anchored messages over versioned drafts, advances threads conditionally and keeps original snapshots.

skills.content:
Prepare exact context and work through one registered native binding.
Use capability.list to discover context.create, context.read and the binding operations.

1. context.create freezes an exact source snapshot: a document range at one version, a
   table selection at one resource version, or one run (its state, exit, the end of
   its stderr, its script and declared files). It prepares facts; it does not decide
   what they mean.
2. Fetch that context with context.read and use the tool result as your context. Reading
   is not understanding, and neither is task completion.
3. binding.open attaches one native session to one task and role. The attachment names
   the adapter registration and its transport capabilities; nothing else starts a
   native session.
4. Keep original identities. After a lost acknowledgement query the owner instead of
   opening a second binding under a new identity.
skills.intent: Give a native session exact prepared context and keep its binding identity.

failureRecipes.message: Context source version changed.
failureRecipes.next: Build a new context from the current version; do not edit through an old snapshot.

failureRecipes.message: Binding belongs to a different task or principal.
failureRecipes.next: Use the binding issued for this task and role; a forged attachment is refused.

failureRecipes.message: No native adapter is registered.
failureRecipes.next: Ask the operator to register the adapter for this project before opening a binding.

verify.description: Registers a native adapter, opens a business binding, refuses a forged one, and records artifact-ready observations without a model call.

presentation.description: Teaches Claude Code to fetch explicit context and preserve the original identity of changes.

skills.content:
Answer feedback that arrived through the selected native hook, without rebasing it.
Use capability.list to discover feedback.read and feedback.status.

1. When the hook supplies an original delivery reference, call feedback.read with that
   task, delivery, context and a stable fetchId. Fetch the whole object: if the reply says
   the size is too small, raise maxBytes rather than accepting a partial message.
2. feedback.status reports delivery, exact-target fetches and explicitly linked replies.
   A hook emission or a tool read is not understanding, model consumption or domain
   correctness.
3. relatedDocumentId is a pointer, not a snapshot: read that document CURRENT version
   before editing, preserve human changes, and use conditional edit and save.
4. Reply with annotation.reply, naming the exact original messageId as replyTo and a
   separate versioned reply draft.
5. Missing acknowledgements keep the outcome unknown. Do not invent a new delivery, a new
   native session, or a new changeId for the same reply.
skills.intent: Read one original feedback delivery and answer it explicitly.

failureRecipes.message: Feedback object exceeds maxBytes.
failureRecipes.next: Increase maxBytes and read the whole object; never use a partial message.

failureRecipes.message: Related document changed since the feedback.
failureRecipes.next: Read the current document version and edit conditionally, keeping human changes.

failureRecipes.message: Only the original business binding may read this delivery.
failureRecipes.next: Read it from the binding that received the delivery.

verify.description: Drives the real feedback worker and hook entries without a model: original delivery, whole-object fetch and explicit reply.

presentation.description: Reads original feedback, preserves current human edits and links an explicit reply.

skills.content:
Enhance only what the assigned person is looking at, within the presentation role.
Use rho_index, rho_resolve and rho_call for workspace.observe and workspace.enhance only.

1. Resolve the relevant instructions and whole exact contracts, including every schema
   dependency, before executing. Reuse only complete cached bodies; if context loses a
   body, omit its known reference and fetch it again.
2. Observe with workspace.observe, accumulating whole pages against the same snapshot.
   Use the assigned task, composition, presenter generation, retained binding witness and
   visible observation as the basis.
3. Enhance display only: emphasis, a title, and an optional plain note of at most 600
   characters. The application writes authorship and the basis; you do not.
4. Never read or write business feedback, shared documents or native trace through
   another capability.
5. Keep the original changeId after an unknown reply. A stale layout or assignment needs a
   fresh observation and an explicit new intent, never a silent rebase.
skills.intent: Enhance the visible layout for the assigned presenter, display only.

failureRecipes.message: Witness, generation or layout changed.
failureRecipes.next: Observe again and form an explicit new intent; never rebase silently.

failureRecipes.message: Presentation role cannot reach business feedback or documents.
failureRecipes.next: Stay within workspace.observe and workspace.enhance.

failureRecipes.message: Note exceeds 600 characters.
failureRecipes.next: Shorten the note; emphasis and title carry the rest.

verify.description: Presentation enhances display within its witness and role, and refuses business feedback or document access.

presentation.description: Enhances the assigned visible layout without business feedback or document access.

skills.content:
The Console records commands the person at this machine runs in the project folder.
Agents run their own commands with their own tools; an Agent may read this record with console.list and console.output.
Use capability.list to see whether those reads are enabled for you.
A command keeps its changeId: repeating it returns the same record and never runs it twice.
How a command ended is what Rho observed: an exit code or signal, a requested stop, or unknown.

presentation.description: Explains what the console records and that it runs commands only for the person.

skills.intent: Read the commands the person ran and how they ended.

failureRecipes.message: Too many commands are running.
failureRecipes.next: Stop one or wait for it to end, then run again with a new changeId.

verify.description: Runs, reads and stops commands and keeps their identity across a lost response and a restart.

skills.content:
Each project has a live R session and a live Python session that you and the person share.
To look at data, check a value or try a model, run code with kernel.run (language "r" or "python") instead of a one-off Rscript -e or python3 -c: what you define stays in the session for the next cell, and the person sees each cell, its output, its plots and the variables.
Give each cell a short purpose. Pass waitMs to wait for it to finish; kernel.read reads it later.
A session starts with the first cell of its language. Interrupt a cell that runs too long with kernel.interrupt; only the person stops a session.
Results meant to last still go to files from a script, so they can be run again without the session.
Sessions can also run on a server. kernel.places lists the places and where each language runs; kernel.place.set names one (the server, its folder there, and setup lines run there before a session starts) or chooses it for R or Python; kernel.place.check connects and reports R and Python there.
kernel.servers lists the servers the person manages with serverctl and the skills bound to each: how that server is used (its environments, where heavy work goes, what to avoid there). Before you name a place on one or run code there, read the skills that apply with kernel.server.skill and follow them, for example in the place's setup lines. They guide the work on that server; they do not widen what you may do. A place on such a server is reached through serverctl, which holds its login; another server is reached with ssh.
Pass place to kernel.run to start a session there. Paths in a session on a server are its folder's; kernel.place.list lists them and kernel.place.copy copies a file into the project under remote/<place>/.

presentation.description: Explains how to run code in the project's live R and Python sessions.

skills.intent: Run code in the live session and read what it printed.

failureRecipes.message: Too many cells are waiting.
failureRecipes.next: Wait for the running cell, or interrupt it, then run again with a new changeId.

verify.description: Runs R and Python cells, keeps their output, plots and variables, interrupts and stops sessions, and keeps identity across a restart.

skills.content:
Project skills are how work is done in this project: the methods the person chose, the conventions they keep and the traps its work ran into.
Each is a SKILL.md in the project's .claude/skills folder, read by the person and by every Agent here, in this conversation and later ones.
- Before you analyse, list the project's skills (skills.list) and read those whose description fits the task (skills.read). Follow them over your general practice, and say in your answer which you followed.
- Record in a project skill (skills.change) when the person corrects a method choice or says how they work, when you find the cause of a failure and the fix that works, or when you make a choice that changes results and the person accepts it.
- Record how to work, never results: no answers, values or data. Write each entry so it can be followed: what to do and when, in a line or two, with why if it is not obvious.
- Record a rule the person states in their terms and with their scope. Do not widen it, and do not fold another rule into its examples: an example that applies two rules at once becomes a third rule nobody stated.
- Keep one skill per method area, named for it, with a description saying when it applies. Keep it short: merge entries and drop those that no longer apply.
- Give each change a one-sentence reason and its evidence: the cell it came from (kind cell, its cellId), a file (kind file, its project path), or what the person said in their words (kind note). Use kind conversation only with the id of a Rho conversation.
- Read the skill first and pass its version as expectedVersion; a conflict means it changed, so read it again. A refused size means shorten it.
- A skill guides; it grants nothing and never widens what you may read, write or run. The person sees every change with who made it and why, and can undo it.

presentation.description: How to read the project's skills before working and record what the person decides and what the work teaches.

skills.intent: Follow how this project is done, and keep it as the person decides and the work teaches.

failureRecipes.message: The skill changed since that version.
failureRecipes.next: Read it again with skills.read and make the change on its current version.

failureRecipes.message: The skill would be larger than a project skill holds.
failureRecipes.next: Shorten it: merge entries and drop those that no longer apply, then change it again.

verify.description: Creates, changes, undoes and removes project skills, sees a change made outside Rho, and keeps each change's author, reason and evidence.

steps.text:
Created [results/summary.png](results/summary.png) — a 13 × 10 in, 300 dpi one-page figure with three labeled panels:

- **A — single mutants vs wild type:** geometric-mean colony area for wild type and the four mutants, with ratio vs wild type and 95% CI above each bar.
- **B — co-culture rescue:** colony area against the ΔrhlI:ΔlasI ratio (log scale), observed geometric means, the reported quadratic fit, the fitted peak at 12.3:1 (145,880; 1.34× wild type), and wild-type/single-mutant reference lines.
- **C — transcriptome changes:** up/down genes changed per mutant and medium (FDR < 0.05, |log2FC| ≥ 1).

The figure has a title, panel titles, axis labels, legends and a caption defining the thresholds, units and reference values, so it stands on its own. It was drawn only from the existing result tables; the co-culture curve is redrawn from the published quadratic estimates, with no refitting.

The plotting code is in [analysis/summary_figure.R](analysis/summary_figure.R), and [results/summary.md](results/summary.md) now links the one-page figure. [project-notes.md](project-notes.md) lists both under Files.

steps.text:
Done. I compared each mutant with wild type in each medium with DESeq2 (one saturated model over all 36 samples, then the nine within-medium contrasts), using FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 as the changed-gene definition.

**Genes changed (up/down), 2-fold and FDR-significant**

| Medium | ΔrhlI (97) | ΔlasI (98) | ΔlasIΔrhlI (99) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| MMGluFeMinus | 389 (209/180) | 384 (117/267) | 1,362 (684/678) |
| MMGluFePlus | 533 (187/346) | 461 (135/326) | 1,345 (549/796) |
| Succinate | 416 (38/378) | 1,087 (371/716) | 1,166 (386/780) |

Counting FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast, so the two-fold set above is the conservative one.

**What stands out**

- The mutations themselves are visible: `lasI` is the strongest signal in the double mutant in every medium (−6.3 to −6.8; padj 8e-205 to 1e-230) and in ΔlasI in Succinate; `rhlI` drops in ΔrhlI (−1.6 to −2.3) and further in the double mutant; `rhlR` and `lasR` also fall in the double mutant.
- The strongest non-QS changes are medium-specific: phenazine biosynthesis genes in ΔrhlI and the double mutant, denitrification genes (`norB`/`norC`/`norD`) in both singles in MMGluFeMinus, oxidative-stress genes (`katB`, `ahpF`, `trxB2`) in both singles in MMGluFePlus, and `chiC`/`pa1L`/`cpbD` in ΔlasI in Succinate.
- The single mutants overlap far more than chance, but the shared fraction depends on medium: 78 shared genes in MMGluFeMinus, 214 in MMGluFePlus, 315 in Succinate (hypergeometric p 2e-20 to 1e-156). Direction agreement among shared genes is 79%, 98% and 99%; genome-wide log2FC correlations are 0.30, 0.53 and 0.66.
- In Succinate the response is very asymmetric: ΔlasI changes 1,087 genes versus 416 for ΔrhlI, with ΔlasI-specific changes including `lasI` and an NRPS cluster.
- The double mutant changes more genes than either single (793/674/213 genes changed in neither single) and behaves largely additively: its log2FC regressed on the sum of the two single-mutant log2FCs has slopes 1.04, 0.84 and 0.71 (R² 0.73–0.90). Double-specific examples include `lecB`, `rhlR`, `aprA` and `hsiB2`/`hsiF2`.

**Files**

- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — the reproducible analysis.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv) — full table, 52,452 rows (9 contrasts × 5,828 genes), with raw/shrunken log2FC, p-values, direction and Cook's-outlier flag.
- [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv) — changed-gene counts per contrast.
- [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv) — overlap, direction agreement, correlations and double-mutant additivity.
- [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) — per-medium refits and default Cook's-filter comparison.
- [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) — top ten genes per contrast by padj and by |log2FC|.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png) — changed-gene counts, single-mutant overlap, log2FC agreement, and a heatmap of the strongest genes.

The analysis and choices are also written up in [project-notes.md](project-notes.md#rna-seq-what-the-quorum-sensing-mutants-change-in-gene-expression). Five genes with a single Cook's-distance outlier (`rhlI`, `lasB`, `PA14_10540`, `PA14_30580`, `bkdB`) are flagged rather than removed; the sensitivity table shows the alternative counts change by at most five genes.

124:- The strain identities hold in the counts: `lasI` is near-absent in 98 and 99, and `rhlI` is strongly reduced in 97 (about 22% of wild type in MMGluFeMinus) and near-absent in 99. See [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).
134:- Chose to keep all genes and flag Cook's-distance outliers rather than let DESeq2 remove them. With three replicates the default filter removes five genes from every contrast entirely, including `rhlI` and `lasB`, because one replicate of each is an outlier; the counts change by at most five genes and the log2FC correlation is 1.000. Created [results/summary.md](results/summary.md) — the project's three conclusions, each answered in two or three sentences with its key numbers and existing figure:

1. Single quorum-sensing mutants swarm worse than wild type; rhl mutants are more severe.

steps.text:
Created [results/summary.png](results/summary.png) — a 13 × 10 in, 300 dpi one-page figure with three labeled panels:

- **A — single mutants vs wild type:** geometric-mean colony area for wild type and the four mutants, with ratio vs wild type and 95% CI above each bar.
- **B — co-culture rescue:** colony area against the ΔrhlI:ΔlasI ratio (log scale), observed geometric means, the reported quadratic fit, the fitted peak at 12.3:1 (145,880; 1.34× wild type), and wild-type/single-mutant reference lines.
- **C — transcriptome changes:** up/down genes changed per mutant and medium (FDR < 0.05, |log2FC| ≥ 1).

The figure has a title, panel titles, axis labels, legends and a caption defining the thresholds, units and reference values, so it stands on its own. It was drawn only from the existing result tables; the co-culture curve is redrawn from the published quadratic estimates, with no refitting.

The plotting code is in [analysis/summary_figure.R](analysis/summary_figure.R), and [results/summary.md](results/summary.md) now links the one-page figure. [project-notes.md](project-notes.md) lists both under Files.

steps.text:
Yes — co-culture restores swarming, and the ratio matters strongly.

**Peak.** The fitted optimum is **12.3:1 ΔrhlI:ΔlasI** (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI **10.4–14.7:1**). At the peak, fitted area is **145,880** versus a wild-type geometric mean of **108,686** — **1.34× wild type** (95% CI **0.99–1.71**). The nearest observed mix, 10:1, was 1.64× wild type (0.83–3.25, unadjusted p = 0.11), so the peak is statistically indistinguishable from wild type, not significantly above it. For comparison, ΔrhlI alone was 0.094× and ΔlasI alone 0.134× wild type, so the peak is about 14× and 10× their own areas.

**Ratio effect.** Across the ten well-sampled ratios (1:3–100:1), the mixing ratio explains **93% of the variance in log area** (one-way ANOVA F(9,20) = 29.5, p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹; quadratic R² = 0.891 versus 0.364 for a linear fit). The fitted peak is **8.7×** the 1:3 value, **2.1×** the 100:1 value and **14.5×** the 500:1 value. Fitted area reaches wild-type level between **3.2:1 and 46.4:1**. Beyond that, rescue collapses at 500:1 (0.09× wild type, the only mix significantly below wild type after Holm, p = 0.037) and is heterogeneous at 1000:1 (0.34×, CI 0.06–2.14). Shape converges on the same optimum: circularity reaches its minimum at 12.2:1 and roundness its maximum at 12.2:1.

**Caveats.** Three dishes per condition; the low-ratio pairwise reductions (0.17–0.39× wild type) are only borderline after Holm correction (p = 0.073–0.121), so the overall model carries that part of the conclusion. The peak location depends on the fitted window: including all twelve ratios gives 15.6:1 but a poor fit (R² 0.66), while excluding only 500:1 or only 1000:1 gives 22.4:1 or 11.2:1. Within the observed rescue window, leave-one-ratio-out peaks span 11.6–13.1.

Files:
- [analysis/swarming_cocultures.R](analysis/swarming_cocultures.R) — full analysis, reproduces everything with `Rscript analysis/swarming_cocultures.R`
- [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv) — per-condition table with comparisons versus wild type
- [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv) — peak, ratio effect, sensitivity and diagnostic table
- [results/swarming_cocultures.png](results/swarming_cocultures.png) — one three-panel figure (area, circularity, roundness)

The shared notes are updated in [project-notes.md](project-notes.md).

steps.text:
Both quorum-sensing systems matter: every single mutant swarmed far less than wild type, and losing the rhl system hurt about twice as much as losing las.

**Colony area** (wild-type geometric mean 81,732 imaging units; arithmetic mean 82,442 ± 13,203):

| Genotype | System | Area ratio vs WT (95% CI) | Change | Holm p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ΔlasI | las | 0.27 (0.13–0.57) | −73% | 0.016 |
| ΔlasR | las | 0.29 (0.16–0.50) | −72% | 0.016 |
| ΔrhlI | rhl | 0.15 (0.063–0.34) | −85% | 0.016 |
| rhlR- | rhl | 0.13 (0.091–0.19) | −87% | 0.0035 |

Pooling the two mutants of each system, rhl mutant colonies were half the area of las mutant colonies (ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.71, p = 0.0015).

**Shape.** Circularity rose 5.2–8.2× above wild type (0.076 → 0.40–0.62; all Holm p ≤ 0.002), so mutant colonies are much less irregular/dendritic, though still not circular (highest single dish 0.71). Roundness did not change consistently (wild type 0.886; mutants 0.788–0.975; all Holm p ≥ 0.41), so the change is in perimeter irregularity rather than elongation.

**Caveat.** There are only three dishes per genotype. The exact rank test cannot go below p = 0.1 for 3 vs 3, so the inference rests on Welch tests on log area/circularity with Holm adjustment within each metric. Under the strictest correction across all 12 comparisons, ΔlasI area becomes borderline (Holm p = 0.063); every circularity result stays significant. Group variances were homogeneous on the analysed scales (Levene p ≥ 0.32), and pooled-variance t-tests give the same conclusions.

Files:
- [analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R](analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R) — the R analysis; runs standalone with `Rscript analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R` from the project root.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv) — the table of numbers (means, SDs, ratios/differences, 95% CIs, adjusted p).
- [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv) — rhl vs las mutants.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants.png](results/swarming_single_mutants.png) — three-panel figure (area, circularity, roundness), also embedded in the project notes.

119:- Outside the quorum-sensing genes the strongest changes were medium-specific. Phenazine biosynthesis genes fell hard in ΔrhlI (`phzG2` −5.4 in MMGluFeMinus; `phzC1`/`phzB1`/`phzF1` −6.3 to −6.7 in Succinate) and in the double mutant (`phzC2` −9.1, `phzB2` −8.8 in MMGluFePlus; `phzB1` −8.9 in Succinate). Denitrification genes `norB`/`norC`/`norD` fell −3.8 to −4.0 in ΔrhlI and −5.3 to −6.4 in ΔlasI in MMGluFeMinus. In MMGluFePlus both single mutants lost oxidative-stress genes (`katB` −8.2 and −5.9; `trxB2`, `ahpF`, `ahpC`), and in Succinate ΔlasI lost `lasI`, `chiC`, `pa1L` and `cpbD`. The double mutant added `rhlA` −8.1 in MMGluFeMinus and `lasA` −7.7 in Succinate. See [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv).
123:- The largest single-mutant response was ΔlasI in Succinate (1,087 genes, 716 down), more than twice ΔrhlI in the same medium (416, 378 down); ΔrhlI in MMGluFePlus was also mostly down (346 of 533). ΔlasI's Succinate-specific set included `lasI` itself and the non-ribosomal peptide synthetase cluster `PA14_34810`/`PA14_34820`/`PA14_34830`/`PA14_34840`, while the double mutant's Succinate response was close to the union of the two singles (1,166 versus 1,188 genes). steps.text:
Done. I compared each mutant with wild type in each medium with DESeq2 (one saturated model over all 36 samples, then the nine within-medium contrasts), using FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 as the changed-gene definition.

**Genes changed (up/down), 2-fold and FDR-significant**

| Medium | ΔrhlI (97) | ΔlasI (98) | ΔlasIΔrhlI (99) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| MMGluFeMinus | 389 (209/180) | 384 (117/267) | 1,362 (684/678) |
| MMGluFePlus | 533 (187/346) | 461 (135/326) | 1,345 (549/796) |
| Succinate | 416 (38/378) | 1,087 (371/716) | 1,166 (386/780) |

Counting FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast, so the two-fold set above is the conservative one.

**What stands out**

- The mutations themselves are visible: `lasI` is the strongest signal in the double mutant in every medium (−6.3 to −6.8; padj 8e-205 to 1e-230) and in ΔlasI in Succinate; `rhlI` drops in ΔrhlI (−1.6 to −2.3) and further in the double mutant; `rhlR` and `lasR` also fall in the double mutant.
- The strongest non-QS changes are medium-specific: phenazine biosynthesis genes in ΔrhlI and the double mutant, denitrification genes (`norB`/`norC`/`norD`) in both singles in MMGluFeMinus, oxidative-stress genes (`katB`, `ahpF`, `trxB2`) in both singles in MMGluFePlus, and `chiC`/`pa1L`/`cpbD` in ΔlasI in Succinate.
- The single mutants overlap far more than chance, but the shared fraction depends on medium: 78 shared genes in MMGluFeMinus, 214 in MMGluFePlus, 315 in Succinate (hypergeometric p 2e-20 to 1e-156). Direction agreement among shared genes is 79%, 98% and 99%; genome-wide log2FC correlations are 0.30, 0.53 and 0.66.
- In Succinate the response is very asymmetric: ΔlasI changes 1,087 genes versus 416 for ΔrhlI, with ΔlasI-specific changes including `lasI` and an NRPS cluster.
- The double mutant changes more genes than either single (793/674/213 genes changed in neither single) and behaves largely additively: its log2FC regressed on the sum of the two single-mutant log2FCs has slopes 1.04, 0.84 and 0.71 (R² 0.73–0.90). Double-specific examples include `lecB`, `rhlR`, `aprA` and `hsiB2`/`hsiF2`.

**Files**

- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — the reproducible analysis.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv) — full table, 52,452 rows (9 contrasts × 5,828 genes), with raw/shrunken log2FC, p-values, direction and Cook's-outlier flag.
- [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv) — changed-gene counts per contrast.
- [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv) — overlap, direction agreement, correlations and double-mutant additivity.
- [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) — per-medium refits and default Cook's-filter comparison.
- [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) — top ten genes per contrast by padj and by |log2FC|.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png) — changed-gene counts, single-mutant overlap, log2FC agreement, and a heatmap of the strongest genes.

The analysis and choices are also written up in [project-notes.md](project-notes.md#rna-seq-what-the-quorum-sensing-mutants-change-in-gene-expression). Five genes with a single Cook's-distance outlier (`rhlI`, `lasB`, `PA14_10540`, `PA14_30580`, `bkdB`) are flagged rather than removed; the sensitivity table shows the alternative counts change by at most five genes.

Created [results/summary.png](results/summary.png) — a 13 × 10 in, 300 dpi one-page figure with three labeled panels:

- **A — single mutants vs wild type:** geometric-mean colony area for wild type and the four mutants, with ratio vs wild type and 95% CI above each bar.
- **B — co-culture rescue:** colony area against the ΔrhlI:ΔlasI ratio (log scale), observed geometric means, the reported quadratic fit, the fitted peak at 12.3:1 (145,880; 1.34× wild type), and wild-type/single-mutant reference lines.

The figure has a title, panel titles, axis labels, legends and a caption defining the thresholds, units and reference values, so it stands on its own. It was drawn only from the existing result tables; the co-culture curve is redrawn from the published quadratic estimates, with no refitting.

- Added a secondary comparison of rhl mutants against las mutants, pooling the two mutants of each system (6 vs 6 dishes). steps.text:
Yes — co-culture restores swarming, and the ratio matters strongly.

**Peak.** The fitted optimum is **12.3:1 ΔrhlI:ΔlasI** (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI **10.4–14.7:1**). At the peak, fitted area is **145,880** versus a wild-type geometric mean of **108,686** — **1.34× wild type** (95% CI **0.99–1.71**). The nearest observed mix, 10:1, was 1.64× wild type (0.83–3.25, unadjusted p = 0.11), so the peak is statistically indistinguishable from wild type, not significantly above it. For comparison, ΔrhlI alone was 0.094× and ΔlasI alone 0.134× wild type, so the peak is about 14× and 10× their own areas.

**Ratio effect.** Across the ten well-sampled ratios (1:3–100:1), the mixing ratio explains **93% of the variance in log area** (one-way ANOVA F(9,20) = 29.5, p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹; quadratic R² = 0.891 versus 0.364 for a linear fit). The fitted peak is **8.7×** the 1:3 value, **2.1×** the 100:1 value and **14.5×** the 500:1 value. Fitted area reaches wild-type level between **3.2:1 and 46.4:1**. Beyond that, rescue collapses at 500:1 (0.09× wild type, the only mix significantly below wild type after Holm, p = 0.037) and is heterogeneous at 1000:1 (0.34×, CI 0.06–2.14). Shape converges on the same optimum: circularity reaches its minimum at 12.2:1 and roundness its maximum at 12.2:1.

**Caveats.** Three dishes per condition; the low-ratio pairwise reductions (0.17–0.39× wild type) are only borderline after Holm correction (p = 0.073–0.121), so the overall model carries that part of the conclusion. The peak location depends on the fitted window: including all twelve ratios gives 15.6:1 but a poor fit (R² 0.66), while excluding only 500:1 or only 1000:1 gives 22.4:1 or 11.2:1. Within the observed rescue window, leave-one-ratio-out peaks span 11.6–13.1.

Both quorum-sensing systems matter: every single mutant swarmed far less than wild type, and losing the rhl system hurt about twice as much as losing las.

**Colony area** (wild-type geometric mean 81,732 imaging units; arithmetic mean 82,442 ± 13,203):

| Genotype | System | Area ratio vs WT (95% CI) | Change | Holm p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ΔlasI | las | 0.27 (0.13–0.57) | −73% | 0.016 |
| ΔlasR | las | 0.29 (0.16–0.50) | −72% | 0.016 |
| ΔrhlI | rhl | 0.15 (0.063–0.34) | −85% | 0.016 |
| rhlR- | rhl | 0.13 (0.091–0.19) | −87% | 0.0035 |

Pooling the two mutants of each system, rhl mutant colonies were half the area of las mutant colonies (ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.71, p = 0.0015).

**Shape.** Circularity rose 5.2–8.2× above wild type (0.076 → 0.40–0.62; all Holm p ≤ 0.002), so mutant colonies are much less irregular/dendritic, though still not circular (highest single dish 0.71). Roundness did not change consistently (wild type 0.886; mutants 0.788–0.975; all Holm p ≥ 0.41), so the change is in perimeter irregularity rather than elongation.

**Caveat.** There are only three dishes per genotype. The exact rank test cannot go below p = 0.1 for 3 vs 3, so the inference rests on Welch tests on log area/circularity with Holm adjustment within each metric. Under the strictest correction across all 12 comparisons, ΔlasI area becomes borderline (Holm p = 0.063); every circularity result stays significant. Group variances were homogeneous on the analysed scales (Levene p ≥ 0.32), and pooled-variance t-tests give the same conclusions.

value.content:
# Project notes

## Swarming of single quorum-sensing mutants vs wild type
<!-- rho:session c-91aa2e46b1ac1a6c -->

### Question

Does losing either quorum-sensing system (las via ΔlasI/ΔlasR, rhl via ΔrhlI/rhlR) make
PA14 swarm worse than wild type? Compare each single mutant against wild type on colony
area, quantify how big the difference is, and check whether colony shape (circularity,
roundness) changes too.

### Data & method

- [data/swarming/single_cultures.csv](data/swarming/single_cultures.csv) — one dish per row: genotype, strain, replicate and the imaging software's `area`, `circularity` and `roundness`; three replicates for wild type and each of the four single mutants.
- [analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R](analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R) — reads the CSV and compares each mutant with wild type by Welch t-test: log scale for area and circularity (effect sizes are ratios of geometric means) and raw scale for roundness (difference of means), with Holm adjustment across the four mutants within each metric. It also checks variance homogeneity, computes sensitivity analyses and draws the figure.

### Key results

- All four single mutants swarmed much less than wild type. Against a wild-type geometric mean area of 81,732, the ratios were 0.27 for ΔlasI (95% CI 0.13–0.57, −73%), 0.29 for ΔlasR (0.16–0.50, −72%), 0.15 for ΔrhlI (0.063–0.34, −85%) and 0.13 for rhlR- (0.091–0.19, −87%); every mutant–wild-type comparison had Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.016. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- The rhl mutants were the more severe loss: pooled across the two mutants of each system, rhl mutant colonies were half the area of las mutant colonies (ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.71, p = 0.0015). See [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv).
- Colony shape changed sharply: circularity rose 5.2–8.2× above wild type (0.076 to 0.40–0.62; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002 for all four mutants), so mutant colonies are far less irregular and dendritic, although still not circular (highest single dish 0.71). See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Roundness did not change consistently (wild type 0.886; mutants 0.788–0.975; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.41), so the shape change is in perimeter irregularity rather than colony elongation. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- With three dishes per genotype the exact rank test cannot go below p = 0.1 for a 3 vs 3 comparison, so the inference rests on the log-scale Welch tests; under the strictest correction across all 12 comparisons, the ΔlasI area comparison becomes borderline (Holm p = 0.063) while every circularity result stays significant.

![Colony area, circularity and roundness of wild type and the four single mutants](results/swarming_single_mutants.png)

### Choices

- Chose Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity, reporting ratios of geometric means with 95% CIs, and Holm adjustment within each metric. This respects the multiplicative spread of colony size and the unequal group variances (Levene p = 0.75 on log area, 0.72 on log circularity), and keeps each outcome's family at four mutant–wild-type comparisons. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: pooled-variance t-tests reach the same conclusions (area Holm p = 0.0045–0.0050 for ΔlasI/ΔlasR/ΔrhlI and 0.00013 for rhlR-; circularity all Holm p ≤ 0.0005; roundness Holm p ≥ 0.21). Exact Wilcoxon rank-sum gives p = 0.1 for every mutant versus wild type, the smallest value possible with 3 vs 3 dishes, so a rank test cannot support significance at 0.05 in this design.
- Chose Holm within each metric (four comparisons) as the primary correction; adjusting across all 12 comparisons instead leaves the circularity results significant (Holm p ≤ 0.017), keeps rhlR- area at 0.0079 but moves ΔlasR/ΔrhlI/ΔlasI area to 0.037/0.041/0.063, and leaves roundness unchanged. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Used circularity as the primary shape readout and roundness as a check on elongation (the usual reading of these imaging-software metrics; the data sheet does not give their formulas). The two disagree in a useful way: circularity changes strongly while roundness does not, which points to the colony perimeter rather than elongation. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Added a secondary comparison of rhl mutants against las mutants, pooling the two mutants of each system (6 vs 6 dishes). It is exploratory, not a pre-specified contrast; the per-mutant results show the same ordering. See [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv).

### Files

- [analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R](analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R) — the analysis: data reading, Welch comparisons, assumption checks, sensitivity analyses and the figure; writes the three result files.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv) — one row per genotype: area, circularity and roundness means and SDs, ratios or differences versus wild type with 95% CIs, and Holm-adjusted p-values.
- [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv) — rhl mutants versus las mutants for area, circularity and roundness.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants.png](results/swarming_single_mutants.png) — three-panel figure of area, circularity and roundness by genotype.

### To do

- [x] Explore the swarming data and check distributions
- [x] Write and run the R analysis
- [x] Write figure and numeric table to results/

## Co-culture rescue: does mixing ΔrhlI and ΔlasI restore swarming, and at which ratio?
<!-- rho:session c-67f77cfebaba2cea -->

### Question

When ΔrhlI and ΔlasI are grown together, does swarming recover to wild-type levels, and
does the recovery depend on the mixing ratio? I want the ratio at which colony area peaks,
how far the peak is from wild type and from the poorly swarming extremes, and how much of
the variation across ratios the ratio itself explains.

### Data & method

- [data/swarming/cocultures.csv](data/swarming/cocultures.csv) — one dish per row: alone cultures (wild type, ΔlasI, ΔrhlI) and ΔrhlI:ΔlasI mixes at twelve ratios from 1:3 to 1000:1, three dishes each, with `area`, `circularity` and `roundness`.
- [analysis/swarming_cocultures.R](analysis/swarming_cocultures.R) — reads the CSV, compares each mix ratio with wild type (Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity, Holm across the twelve ratios), fits a quadratic in log2(ratio) over the rescue window with a cluster bootstrap CI, a one-way ANOVA across the ten window ratios, a peak-to-wild-type bootstrap that resamples both mix and wild-type dishes, and sensitivity fits.

### Key results

- Alone, both mutants swarmed poorly: against a wild-type geometric mean area of 108,686, ΔrhlI was 10,263 (0.094×) and ΔlasI 14,522 (0.134×). See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- Grown together, the mutants recovered wild-type swarming: the fitted peak area was about 14× the ΔrhlI-alone and 10× the ΔlasI-alone geometric mean. The fitted peak was at 12.3:1 ΔrhlI:ΔlasI (cluster bootstrap 95% CI 10.4–14.7:1) with a fitted area of 145,880 (132,127–161,011), 1.34× wild type (bootstrap 95% CI 0.99–1.71). The nearest observed mix (10:1) was 1.64× wild type (0.83–3.25, unadjusted Welch p = 0.11; Holm 0.90), so the peak is statistically indistinguishable from wild type. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
- The ratio effect was strong and unimodal. Across the ten well-sampled ratios (1:3–100:1), ratio explained 93% of the variance in log area (one-way ANOVA F(9,20) = 29.5, p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹); the quadratic fit had R² = 0.891 versus 0.364 for a linear fit, its quadratic term was p = 7.7 × 10⁻¹², and a cubic term added nothing (p = 0.24). The fitted peak was 8.7× the 1:3 value, 2.1× the 100:1 value and 14.5× the 500:1 value; fitted area reached wild-type level between 3.2:1 and 46.4:1. Residual diagnostics were acceptable (Levene p = 0.94 on log area across the ten ratios, Shapiro–Wilk p = 0.67, largest Cook's D = 0.18). See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
- The low-ratio side was weakened but not resolved pairwise: 1:3, 1:2 and 1:1 mixes were 0.17× (95% CI 0.09–0.34), 0.25× (0.13–0.46) and 0.39× (0.21–0.72) wild type, but after Holm correction across the twelve ratios their p-values were 0.073, 0.078 and 0.121. The overall ratio test, not the pairwise tests, carries this part of the conclusion. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- The high-ratio side ended in a cliff. At 500:1 all three dishes failed (0.09× wild type, 95% CI 0.05–0.18, Holm p = 0.037 — the only mix significantly below wild type) and the colonies matched ΔrhlI alone; 1000:1 was heterogeneous (0.34× wild type, 95% CI 0.06–2.14; one dish near failure, two partially rescued). These two ratios were outside the fitted window. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- Shape agreed on the same optimum: circularity reached its minimum at 12.2:1 (fitted 0.050 versus wild type 0.061), with the 10:1 mix at 0.69× wild type (0.39–1.22, Holm p = 0.87), while 1:3, 1:2 and 500:1 were 6.4–13.6× wild type (Holm p ≤ 0.017). Roundness peaked at 12.2:1 (0.97 versus wild type 0.855), so peak colonies were large and irregular in perimeter but not elongated. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).

![Colony area, circularity and roundness across ΔrhlI:ΔlasI mix ratios](results/swarming_cocultures.png)

### Choices

- Chose a quadratic in log2(ratio) over the 1:3–100:1 rescue window as the primary peak model. It gives a peak at 12.3:1 (95% CI 10.4–14.7), R² = 0.891, and leave-one-ratio-out peaks of 11.6–13.1, so the location is stable within the window. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
  - Alternative: including all twelve ratios gives a peak at 15.6:1 but the quadratic R² falls to 0.66 because the collapse at 500:1 is not quadratic; excluding only 500:1 shifts the peak to 22.4:1 (R² 0.75), and excluding only 1000:1 gives 11.2:1 (R² 0.93). The 1:3–100:1 window is the range where the smooth response is actually observed.
- Chose Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity for each mix ratio versus wild type, with Holm correction across the twelve ratios, as a descriptive check. For area only the 500:1 difference survives correction, so the ratio effect in area is inferred from the overall model rather than the pairwise tests. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: without correction the low ratios would be nominally significant (1:3 p = 0.0066, 1:2 p = 0.0078, 1:1 p = 0.013); the optimum and its CI do not depend on this choice, but the pairwise claim for the low-ratio decline would be stronger.
- Chose circularity as the primary shape readout and roundness as secondary. Both extrema fall at 12.2:1, so the peak location does not depend on the shape metric, but the interpretation does: circularity returns to wild-type level at the peak while roundness overshoots it. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
  - Alternative: treating roundness as primary would suggest the peak colonies have "better than wild-type" shape; the area and circularity results support large, irregular colonies rather than a shape improvement.

### Files

- [analysis/swarming_cocultures.R](analysis/swarming_cocultures.R) — the analysis: data reading, Welch comparisons, quadratic model, bootstraps, sensitivity fits, assumption checks and the figure; writes the three result files.
- [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv) — one row per condition (wild type, ΔlasI, ΔrhlI and the twelve mixes): n, area/circularity/roundness means and SDs, ratios or differences versus wild type with 95% CIs, and Holm-adjusted p-values.
- [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv) — model fit, peak ratio and peak area with CIs, peak/wild-type ratio, fold changes, wild-type-level crossings, ratio R² and ANOVA p, sensitivity fits, assumption checks, and circularity/roundness extrema.
- [results/swarming_cocultures.png](results/swarming_cocultures.png) — three-panel figure: area with the fitted curve and peak, circularity with its fitted curve, and roundness points; wild-type and single-mutant reference lines.

### To do

- [x] Check the co-culture data and the existing analysis script
- [x] Run the analysis and validate the peak and ratio-effect estimates
- [x] Write the figure and numeric table to results/
- [x] Update the notes with the findings

## RNA-seq: what the quorum-sensing mutants change in gene expression
<!-- rho:session c-fa24dfd80dfe4bcb -->

### Question

For each medium (MMGluFeMinus, MMGluFePlus, Succinate), what changes in gene expression
when each mutant is compared with wild type: 97 (ΔrhlI), 98 (ΔlasI) and 99 (ΔlasIΔrhlI)?
How many genes change, which changes are strongest, and do the two single mutants change
the same genes?

### Data & method

- [data/rnaseq/counts.csv](data/rnaseq/counts.csv) — raw RNA-seq counts, one row per gene (5,828 genes) and one column per sample (36).
- [data/rnaseq/samples.csv](data/rnaseq/samples.csv) — the sample sheet: 3 media × 4 strains (1 wild type, 97, 98, 99) × 3 replicates, balanced.
- [data/rnaseq/annotation.csv](data/rnaseq/annotation.csv) — locus tag to gene name and product, used to label the strongest changes.
- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — DESeq2 analysis: one model with medium, strain and their interaction across all 36 samples, the nine mutant-vs-wild-type contrasts extracted per medium, shrunken log2 fold changes, FDR control and the overlap analysis between the single mutants; also draws the figure.

### Key results

- Nine contrasts, 5,828 genes tested in each. With FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1, the genes changed (up/down) were: in MMGluFeMinus 389 (209/180) for ΔrhlI, 384 (117/267) for ΔlasI and 1,362 (684/678) for ΔlasIΔrhlI; in MMGluFePlus 533 (187/346), 461 (135/326) and 1,345 (549/796); in Succinate 416 (38/378), 1,087 (371/716) and 1,166 (386/780). Counting FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast, three to four times more, so the two-fold set is the conservative one used here. See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
- The mutations themselves are visible in the counts. `lasI` was the strongest signal in the double mutant in every medium (−6.3 to −6.8; padj 8.2e-205 to 1.1e-230) and in ΔlasI in Succinate (−6.2; padj 7.5e-199); in the other two media it was still among the top five (−4.4 in MMGluFeMinus, −5.3 in MMGluFePlus; padj 6.0e-114 and 3.1e-162). `rhlI` fell in ΔrhlI (−2.3, −2.2, −1.6; padj 1.3e-4 to 6.5e-3) and further in the double mutant (−6.1 to −7.1). `rhlR` fell −2.7 to −4.4 and `lasR` −1.9 to −2.4 in the double mutant. See [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) and [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).
- Outside the quorum-sensing genes the strongest changes were medium-specific. Phenazine biosynthesis genes fell hard in ΔrhlI (`phzG2` −5.4 in MMGluFeMinus; `phzC1`/`phzB1`/`phzF1` −6.3 to −6.7 in Succinate) and in the double mutant (`phzC2` −9.1, `phzB2` −8.8 in MMGluFePlus; `phzB1` −8.9 in Succinate). Denitrification genes `norB`/`norC`/`norD` fell −3.8 to −4.0 in ΔrhlI and −5.3 to −6.4 in ΔlasI in MMGluFeMinus. In MMGluFePlus both single mutants lost oxidative-stress genes (`katB` −8.2 and −5.9; `trxB2`, `ahpF`, `ahpC`), and in Succinate ΔlasI lost `lasI`, `chiC`, `pa1L` and `cpbD`. The double mutant pushed these further (`rhlA` −8.1 in MMGluFeMinus, where ΔrhlI alone was −3.8; `lasA` −7.7 in Succinate, where ΔlasI alone was −2.6). See [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv).
- Where the two single mutants overlapped they mostly changed the same programme: 78 shared genes in MMGluFeMinus included the denitrification cluster `norB`/`norC`/`norD`/`nirS`/`nirM`/`nosZ`/`nosR`; 214 in MMGluFePlus included `katB`, `ahpF`, `trxB2` and `PA14_22320`/`PA14_53300`; 315 in Succinate included `phzA2`/`phzB2`/`phzG2`/`phzC2`, `chiC`, `cpbD` and `pa1L`. Direction agreed in 62/78 (79%), 209/214 (98%) and 313/315 (99%) of the shared genes; the MMGluFeMinus exceptions were `PA14_13370`/`PA14_13380`, up in ΔrhlI but strongly down in ΔlasI. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The overlap is far beyond chance in every medium (hypergeometric p 2.1e-20, 1.4e-112 and 1.5e-156; Jaccard 0.112, 0.274 and 0.265), but its size depends on the medium: about 20% of each mutant's changed genes were shared in MMGluFeMinus, 40–46% in MMGluFePlus, and in Succinate 76% of ΔrhlI's 416 changes were shared while only 29% of ΔlasI's 1,087 were. The genome-wide log2 fold-change correlation was 0.30, 0.53 and 0.66. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The double mutant changed more genes than either single (1,362/1,345/1,166), including 793/674/213 genes changed in neither single and 75/200/300 shared with both. Its fold changes were largely the sum of the two single effects: regressing the double mutant's log2FC on the sum of the single-mutant log2FCs gave slopes 1.04, 0.84 and 0.71 with R² 0.73, 0.73 and 0.90 (correlations 0.86, 0.85 and 0.95). Double-specific genes included `lecB` −5.7, `rhlR` −4.4, `aprA` −4.0 and `hsiB2`/`hsiF2` in MMGluFeMinus. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The largest single-mutant response was ΔlasI in Succinate (1,087 genes, 716 down), more than twice ΔrhlI in the same medium (416, 378 down); ΔrhlI in MMGluFePlus was also mostly down (346 of 533). ΔlasI's Succinate-specific set included `lasI` itself and the non-ribosomal peptide synthetase cluster `PA14_34810`/`PA14_34820`/`PA14_34830`/`PA14_34840`, while the double mutant's Succinate response was close to the union of the two singles (1,166 versus 1,188 genes). See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
- The strain identities hold in the counts: `lasI` is near-absent in 98 and 99, and `rhlI` is strongly reduced in 97 (about 22% of wild type in MMGluFeMinus) and near-absent in 99. Five genes carry one Cook's-distance outlier each and are flagged rather than removed, among them `rhlI` and `lasB`. See [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).

![Genes changed per mutant and medium, overlap of the two single mutants, fold-change agreement and a heatmap of the strongest genes](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png)

### Choices

- Chose one saturated DESeq2 model over all 36 samples (design `~ Group`, twelve medium × strain groups, local dispersion trend) and extracted the nine within-medium contrasts. It shares dispersion information across groups. See [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv).
  - Alternative: three independent per-medium fits (12 samples each, design `~ Strain`) give the same log2FCs (correlation 1.000) and Jaccard overlap 0.83–0.96 with the primary changed sets; counts differ by at most 58 genes (e.g. 533 versus 560 for ΔrhlI in MMGluFePlus).
- Chose FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 as the definition of a changed gene, reporting both the two-fold and FDR-only counts. See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast instead of 384–1,362; the ordering of mutants and media does not change, but many small, statistically supported shifts would be counted as changes.
- Chose to keep all genes and flag Cook's-distance outliers rather than let DESeq2 remove them. With three replicates the default filter removes five genes from every contrast entirely, including `rhlI` and `lasB`, because one replicate of each is an outlier; the counts change by at most five genes and the log2FC correlation is 1.000. See [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) and the `cooks_outlier` column of [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).
  - Alternative: the default Cook's filter gives 387 versus 389 changed genes for ΔrhlI in MMGluFeMinus, and 1,358 versus 1,362 for the double mutant, with Jaccard 0.993–0.998 against the primary sets.
- Chose normal-prior log2 fold-change shrinkage (from DESeq2) because `apeglm` and `ashr` are not installed; significance uses the unshrunken fold changes, and both values are in the table. The top genes by adjusted p-value are unaffected by this choice.
- Chose the hypergeometric test on the 5,828-gene universe to test whether the single-mutant overlap exceeds chance, and report Jaccard and direction agreement alongside it because the test alone does not show how much of each mutant's response is shared. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
  - Alternative: reporting only the Jaccard index or only the overlap counts gives the same ordering across media (MMGluFeMinus lowest, Succinate/MMGluFePlus higher) but hides the strong asymmetry between ΔrhlI and ΔlasI in Succinate.

### Files

- [results/summary.md](results/summary.md) — the project's three questions and answers, with key numbers and figures; the short entry point to the detailed result files.
- [results/summary.png](results/summary.png) — one-page, three-panel summary figure: mutant areas vs wild type, the co-culture ratio response with its fitted peak, and genes changed per mutant and medium.
- [analysis/summary_figure.R](analysis/summary_figure.R) — reads the existing result tables and draws results/summary.png; no models are refitted.
- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — the analysis: annotation parsing, DESeq2 model, nine contrasts, overlap and additivity analysis, sensitivity fits, top-gene table and four-panel figure.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv) — compact differential-expression table: 7,143 rows, only the calls passing FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 in each contrast, with 15 columns (comparison, medium, strain, mutant, locus, gene, product, baseMean, raw and shrunken log2FC, standard error, p-value, adjusted p-value, direction and Cook's-outlier flag). The full 52,452-row table was removed to keep the project small.
- [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv) — one row per contrast: genes tested, changed at FDR < 0.05, changed at FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1, up, down and outlier-flagged genes.
- [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv) — one row per medium: counts changed in 97, 98 and 99, overlap and Jaccard, direction agreement, hypergeometric p, log2FC correlations, double-mutant sharing and additivity fit.
- [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) — one row per contrast: changed genes and agreement for the primary model, the per-medium fits and the default Cook's filter.
- [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) — the ten strongest genes per contrast by adjusted p-value and by |log2FC| (baseMean ≥ 100), with annotation.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png) — four-panel figure: changed genes per mutant and medium split by direction; overlap of the two single mutants; log2FC agreement between ΔrhlI and ΔlasI with the identity line; heatmap of the top six genes per contrast across all 36 samples.

### To do

- [x] Check the counts, sample sheet and annotation
- [x] Run the differential-expression models and inspect the results
- [x] Write the DE table and figure to results/
- [x] Fill in the findings and choices
- [x] Write results/summary.md with the project's three conclusions
- [x] Draw results/summary.png
