# Effect sizes, shape model and rescue window
eta2 <- function(d) { a <- aov(log(area) ~ factor(ratio), data = d); s <- summary(a)[[1]][["Sum Sq"]]; s[1]/sum(s) }
cat("one-way R2 among mix ratios, window:", round(eta2(win), 4),
    " all 12 ratios:", round(eta2(mix), 4), "\n")
cat("quadratic model residual SD (log scale):", round(summary(m2)$sigma, 4),
    " df:", summary(m2)$df[2], "\n")
m3 <- lm(log(area) ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3), data = win)
cat("cubic term p:", signif(anova(m2, m3)$`Pr(>F)`[2], 3), " cubic R2:", round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 4), "\n")

# Circularity on log scale, same window (minimum = smoothest colonies)
cm2 <- lm(log(circularity) ~ x + I(x^2), data = win)
ccf <- coef(cm2)
cat("circularity quadratic R2:", round(summary(cm2)$r.squared, 4),
    " minimum at ratio:", round(2^(-ccf[2]/(2*ccf[3])), 2),
    " fitted min:", round(exp(predict(cm2, newdata = data.frame(x = -ccf[2]/(2*ccf[3])))), 3),
    " | WT:", round(exp(mean(log(wt_circ))), 3), "\n")

# Observed peak mix (10:1) against each single mutant and wild type
p10 <- subset(mix, ratio == 10)
for (grp in c("ΔrhlI", "ΔlasI", "wild type")) {
  ref <- coc$area[coc$culture == grp]
  tt <- t.test(log(p10$area), log(ref))
  cat("10:1 vs", grp, ": ratio", round(exp(unname(tt$estimate[1] - tt$estimate[2])), 2),
      " CI", paste(round(exp(tt$conf.int), 2), collapse = "-"), " p", signif(tt$p.value, 3), "\n")
}

# Rescue window: where the fitted curve is at or above the wild-type geometric mean
lv <- log(exp(mean(log(wt_area))))
cf <- coef(m2)
roots <- polyroot(c(cf[1] - lv, cf[2], cf[3]))
roots <- Re(roots[abs(Im(roots)) < 1e-8])
cat("fitted area reaches WT gm between ratios:", paste(round(2^sort(roots), 2), collapse = " and "), "\n")
cat("fitted area at 2:1:", round(exp(predict(m2, newdata = data.frame(x = 1))), 0),
    " 3:1:", round(exp(predict(m2, newdata = data.frame(x = log2(3)))), 0),
    " 5:1:", round(exp(predict(m2, newdata = data.frame(x = log2(5)))), 0), "\n")

# Peak value with bootstrap CI (cluster bootstrap, same draws as before)
set.seed(1)
boot_peak_val <- replicate(5000, {
  idx <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(win)), win$ratio), function(i) sample(i, length(i), replace = TRUE)))
  d <- win[idx, ]
  cf <- coef(lm(log(area) ~ x + I(x^2), data = d))
  if (is.na(cf[3]) || cf[3] >= 0) NA_real_ else exp(cf[1] - cf[2]^2/(4*cf[3]))
})
cat("fitted peak area bootstrap median and 95% CI:",
    paste(round(quantile(boot_peak_val, c(.5, .025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)), collapse = "  "), "\n")

# Peak with 1000:1 excluded but 500:1 included, and vice versa
for (lab in c("excl1000", "excl500", "exclBoth")) {
  d <- switch(lab,
    excl1000 = subset(mix, ratio != 1000),
    excl500  = subset(mix, ratio != 500),
    exclBoth = subset(mix, ratio != 500 & ratio != 1000))
  cf2 <- coef(lm(log(area) ~ x + I(x^2), data = d))
  cat(lab, ": peak", round(2^(-cf2[2]/(2*cf2[3])), 2), " R2", round(summary(lm(log(area) ~ x + I(x^2), data = d))$r.squared, 3), "\n")
}

# Pooled-variance sensitivity for mix vs WT, Holm across 12 ratios
ratios <- sort(unique(mix$ratio))
pooled_p <- function(var, tf) {
  wt <- tf(coc[[var]][coc$culture == "wild type"])
  sapply(ratios, function(r) {
    x <- tf(mix[[var]][mix$ratio == r])
    t.test(x, wt, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
  })
}
pa <- p.adjust(pooled_p("area", log), "holm")
pc <- p.adjust(pooled_p("circularity", log), "holm")
pr <- p.adjust(pooled_p("roundness", identity), "holm")
print(data.frame(ratio = ratios, area_pooled_holm = signif(pa, 3),
                 circ_pooled_holm = signif(pc, 3), round_pooled_holm = signif(pr, 3)),
      row.names = FALSE)

dups <- unique(annot$locus_tag[duplicated(annot$locus_tag)])
cat("duplicated loci:", length(dups), "\n")
print(annot[annot$locus_tag %in% head(dups, 6), ])

# one annotation row per locus: first non-empty gene name, first product
annot_u <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(annot, annot$locus_tag), function(d) {
  g <- d$gene[!is.na(d$gene) & d$gene != "" & d$gene != "-"]
  p <- d$product[!is.na(d$product) & d$product != ""]
  data.frame(locus_tag = d$locus_tag[1],
             gene = if (length(g)) g[1] else "",
             product = if (length(p)) p[1] else "",
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(annot_u) <- annot_u$locus_tag
cat("unique annotation rows:", nrow(annot_u), "\n")

# align counts to sample sheet
counts <- counts[, samples$AzentaName]
meta <- samples
rownames(meta) <- meta$AzentaName
meta$Strain <- factor(meta$Strain, levels = c(1, 97, 98, 99))
meta$Media <- factor(meta$Media, levels = c("MMGluFeMinus", "MMGluFePlus", "Succinate"))
meta$Group <- factor(paste(meta$Media, meta$Strain, sep = "_"))
cat("aligned:", identical(colnames(counts), rownames(meta)), "\n")

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts, colData = meta, design = ~ Media * Strain)
cat("genes before filter:", nrow(dds), "\n")
keep <- rowSums(counts >= 10) >= 3
dds <- dds[keep, ]
cat("genes with >=10 counts in >=3 samples:", nrow(dds), "\n")
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
pca <- prcomp(t(assay(vsd)))
pv <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1)
cat("variance explained PC1-4:", pv[1:4], "\n")
pd <- data.frame(meta, PC1 = pca$x[,1], PC2 = pca$x[,2])
print(aggregate(cbind(PC1, PC2) ~ Media + Strain, pd, mean), digits = 1)
p1 <- ggplot(pd, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = Strain, shape = Media)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + theme_bw() +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", pv[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", pv[2], "%)"), title = "VST PCA, all samples")
print(p1)

lines <- readLines("data/rnaseq/annotation.csv")
parts <- strsplit(lines[-1], ",", fixed = TRUE)
annot2 <- data.frame(
  locus_tag = vapply(parts, `[`, "", 1),
  gene      = vapply(parts, function(x) if (length(x) >= 2) x[2] else "", ""),
  product   = vapply(parts, function(x) if (length(x) >= 3) paste(x[-(1:2)], collapse = ",") else "", ""),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat("rows:", nrow(annot2), " loci unique:", length(unique(annot2$locus_tag)), "\n")
cat("bad locus tags:", sum(!grepl("^PA14_[0-9]+$", annot2$locus_tag)), "\n")
cat("named genes:", sum(annot2$gene != ""), "\n")
print(annot2[annot2$gene %in% c("lasI","lasR","rhlI","rhlR","pqsA","pqsR"), ])

# quorum-sensing gene counts per group
qs <- annot2$locus_tag[annot2$gene %in% c("lasI","lasR","rhlI","rhlR")]
qs <- intersect(qs, rownames(counts))
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(qs, function(g) {
  data.frame(locus = g, gene = annot2$gene[match(g, annot2$locus_tag)],
             meta[, c("Media","Strain")], count = counts[g, ])
}))
agg <- aggregate(count ~ Media + Strain + gene + locus, long, mean)
print(reshape(agg, idvar = c("Media","gene","locus"), timevar = "Strain", direction = "wide"), digits = 0)

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))
group_levels <- as.vector(t(outer(levels(meta$Media), c("1","97","98","99"), paste, sep = "_")))
meta$Group <- factor(paste(meta$Media, meta$Strain, sep = "_"), levels = group_levels)
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts, colData = meta, design = ~ Group)
cat("genes:", nrow(dds), " samples:", ncol(dds), " groups:", nlevels(dds$Group), "\n")
cat("size factors:\n"); print(round(sizeFactors(dds), 3))
dds <- DESeq(dds, fitType = "local", quiet = TRUE)
cat("dispersion summary:\n"); print(summary(dispersions(dds)))
cat("dispersion trend:"); print(attr(dispersionFunction(dds), "fitType"))

res_list <- list()
summ <- list()
for (medium in levels(meta$Media)) {
  for (mut in c("97","98","99")) {
    con <- c("Group", paste(medium, mut, sep = "_"), paste(medium, "1", sep = "_"))
    r <- results(dds, contrast = con, alpha = 0.05)
    rs <- lfcShrink(dds, contrast = con, type = "normal")
    key <- paste(medium, mut, sep = "_")
    df <- data.frame(locus_tag = rownames(r), baseMean = r$baseMean,
                     log2FC = r$log2FoldChange, lfcSE = r$lfcSE, stat = r$stat,
                     pvalue = r$pvalue, padj = r$padj,
                     log2FC_shrunk = rs$log2FoldChange, lfcSE_shrunk = rs$lfcSE)
    df$gene <- annot2$gene[match(df$locus_tag, annot2$locus_tag)]
    df$product <- annot2$product[match(df$locus_tag, annot2$locus_tag)]
    res_list[[key]] <- df
    sig <- !is.na(df$padj) & df$padj < 0.05
    sig2 <- sig & abs(df$log2FC) >= 1
    summ[[key]] <- data.frame(comparison = key, tested = sum(!is.na(df$padj)),
                              FDR05 = sum(sig), FDR05_2fold = sum(sig2),
                              up = sum(sig2 & df$log2FC > 0), down = sum(sig2 & df$log2FC < 0))
  }
}
summ <- do.call(rbind, summ)
print(summ, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\ntop 3 by padj per contrast:\n")
for (k in names(res_list)) {
  d <- res_list[[k]]
  d <- d[!is.na(d$padj) & d$padj < 0.05, ]
  d <- head(d[order(d$padj), ], 3)
  cat("\n", k, "\n")
  print(data.frame(gene = d$gene, locus = d$locus_tag, log2FC = round(d$log2FC, 2), padj = signif(d$padj, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
}

sigset <- function(k, fold = TRUE) {
  d <- res_list[[k]]
  ok <- !is.na(d$padj) & d$padj < 0.05
  if (fold) ok <- ok & abs(d$log2FC) >= 1
  d$locus_tag[ok]
}
universe <- sum(!is.na(res_list[[1]]$padj))
cat("universe tested:", universe, "\n\n")
ov <- list()
for (m in levels(meta$Media)) {
  a <- sigset(paste(m,"97",sep="_")); b <- sigset(paste(m,"98",sep="_")); d99 <- sigset(paste(m,"99",sep="_"))
  both <- intersect(a, b); only97 <- setdiff(a, b); only98 <- setdiff(b, a)
  da <- res_list[[paste(m,"97",sep="_")]]; db <- res_list[[paste(m,"98",sep="_")]]
  dir_ok <- sum(sign(da$log2FC[match(both, da$locus_tag)]) == sign(db$log2FC[match(both, db$locus_tag)]))
  unionab <- union(a, b)
  p_hyper <- phyper(length(both) - 1, length(a), universe - length(a), length(b), lower.tail = FALSE)
  ov[[m]] <- data.frame(media = m, n97 = length(a), n98 = length(b), both = length(both),
                        only97 = length(only97), only98 = length(only98),
                        jaccard = round(length(both)/length(unionab), 3),
                        same_direction = dir_ok,
                        p_overlap = signif(p_hyper, 3),
                        n99 = length(d99), n99_in_union = sum(d99 %in% unionab),
                        n99_new = sum(!d99 %in% unionab))
  cat(m, ": union singles =", length(unionab), "; 99 DE in union =", sum(d99 %in% unionab),
      "; 99 DE not in either single =", sum(!d99 %in% unionab), "\n")
  cat("  LFC correlation all genes:", round(cor(da$log2FC, db$log2FC, use = "complete.obs"), 3),
      "; among union:", round(cor(da$log2FC[match(unionab, da$locus_tag)], db$log2FC[match(unionab, db$locus_tag)]), 3), "\n")
}
ov <- do.call(rbind, ov)
print(ov, row.names = FALSE)

cat("\nquorum-sensing genes in the contrasts:\n")
for (k in names(res_list)) {
  d <- res_list[[k]]
  d <- d[d$locus_tag %in% qs, ]
  cat(k, ": ", paste(paste0(d$gene, " ", round(d$log2FC, 1), " (padj ", signif(d$padj, 2), ")"), collapse = "; "), "\n")
}

cat("\ntop products among padj < 1e-50 (unique genes):\n")
alltop <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res_list), function(k) {
  d <- res_list[[k]]; d <- d[!is.na(d$padj) & d$padj < 1e-50, ]
  data.frame(comparison = k, d[, c("locus_tag","gene","product","log2FC","padj")])
}))
alltop <- alltop[!duplicated(alltop$locus_tag), ]
print(head(alltop[order(alltop$padj), ], 20), row.names = FALSE)

cat("\nlargest |log2FC| among DE (FDR<0.05, |LFC|>=1, baseMean>=100), top 5 per contrast:\n")
for (k in names(res_list)) {
  d <- res_list[[k]]; d <- d[!is.na(d$padj) & d$padj < 0.05 & abs(d$log2FC) >= 1 & d$baseMean >= 100, ]
  d <- head(d[order(-abs(d$log2FC)), ], 5)
  cat("\n", k, "\n")
  print(data.frame(locus = d$locus_tag, gene = d$gene, log2FC = round(d$log2FC, 1), baseMean = round(d$baseMean), padj = signif(d$padj, 2)), row.names = FALSE)
}

    alt[[key]] <- data.frame(locus_tag = rownames(r), log2FC = r$log2FoldChange, padj = r$padj)
    p <- res_list[[key]]
    sig_p <- !is.na(p$padj) & p$padj < 0.05 & abs(p$log2FC) >= 1
    sig_a <- !is.na(r$padj) & r$padj < 0.05 & abs(r$log2FoldChange) >= 1
    cmp[[key]] <- data.frame(comparison = key, primary = sum(sig_p), per_medium = sum(sig_a),
                             shared = sum(sig_p & sig_a), jaccard = round(sum(sig_p & sig_a)/sum(sig_p | sig_a), 3),
                             lfc_cor = round(cor(p$log2FC, r$log2FoldChange, use = "complete.obs"), 3))
  }
}
print(do.call(rbind, cmp), row.names = FALSE)

value.content:
# Project notes

## Swarming of single quorum-sensing mutants vs wild type
<!-- rho:session c-91aa2e46b1ac1a6c -->

### Question

Does losing either quorum-sensing system (las via ΔlasI/ΔlasR, rhl via ΔrhlI/rhlR) make
PA14 swarm worse than wild type? Compare each single mutant against wild type on colony
area, quantify how big the difference is, and check whether colony shape (circularity,
roundness) changes too.

### Data & method

- [data/swarming/single_cultures.csv](data/swarming/single_cultures.csv) — one dish per row: genotype, strain, replicate and the imaging software's `area`, `circularity` and `roundness`; three replicates for wild type and each of the four single mutants.
- [analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R](analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R) — reads the CSV and compares each mutant with wild type by Welch t-test: log scale for area and circularity (effect sizes are ratios of geometric means) and raw scale for roundness (difference of means), with Holm adjustment across the four mutants within each metric. It also checks variance homogeneity, computes sensitivity analyses and draws the figure.

### Key results

- All four single mutants swarmed much less than wild type. Against a wild-type geometric mean area of 81,732, the ratios were 0.27 for ΔlasI (95% CI 0.13–0.57, −73%), 0.29 for ΔlasR (0.16–0.50, −72%), 0.15 for ΔrhlI (0.063–0.34, −85%) and 0.13 for rhlR- (0.091–0.19, −87%); every mutant–wild-type comparison had Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.016. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- The rhl mutants were the more severe loss: pooled across the two mutants of each system, rhl mutant colonies were half the area of las mutant colonies (ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.35–0.71, p = 0.0015). See [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv).
- Colony shape changed sharply: circularity rose 5.2–8.2× above wild type (0.076 to 0.40–0.62; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002 for all four mutants), so mutant colonies are far less irregular and dendritic, although still not circular (highest single dish 0.71). See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Roundness did not change consistently (wild type 0.886; mutants 0.788–0.975; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.41), so the shape change is in perimeter irregularity rather than colony elongation. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- With three dishes per genotype the exact rank test cannot go below p = 0.1 for a 3 vs 3 comparison, so the inference rests on the log-scale Welch tests; under the strictest correction across all 12 comparisons, the ΔlasI area comparison becomes borderline (Holm p = 0.063) while every circularity result stays significant.

![Colony area, circularity and roundness of wild type and the four single mutants](results/swarming_single_mutants.png)

### Choices

- Chose Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity, reporting ratios of geometric means with 95% CIs, and Holm adjustment within each metric. This respects the multiplicative spread of colony size and the unequal group variances (Levene p = 0.75 on log area, 0.72 on log circularity), and keeps each outcome's family at four mutant–wild-type comparisons. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: pooled-variance t-tests reach the same conclusions (area Holm p = 0.0045–0.0050 for ΔlasI/ΔlasR/ΔrhlI and 0.00013 for rhlR-; circularity all Holm p ≤ 0.0005; roundness Holm p ≥ 0.21). Exact Wilcoxon rank-sum gives p = 0.1 for every mutant versus wild type, the smallest value possible with 3 vs 3 dishes, so a rank test cannot support significance at 0.05 in this design.
- Chose Holm within each metric (four comparisons) as the primary correction; adjusting across all 12 comparisons instead leaves the circularity results significant (Holm p ≤ 0.017), keeps rhlR- area at 0.0079 but moves ΔlasR/ΔrhlI/ΔlasI area to 0.037/0.041/0.063, and leaves roundness unchanged. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Used circularity as the primary shape readout and roundness as a check on elongation (the usual reading of these imaging-software metrics; the data sheet does not give their formulas). The two disagree in a useful way: circularity changes strongly while roundness does not, which points to the colony perimeter rather than elongation. See [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv).
- Added a secondary comparison of rhl mutants against las mutants, pooling the two mutants of each system (6 vs 6 dishes). It is exploratory, not a pre-specified contrast; the per-mutant results show the same ordering. See [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv).

### Files

- [analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R](analysis/swarming_single_mutants.R) — the analysis: data reading, Welch comparisons, assumption checks, sensitivity analyses and the figure; writes the three result files.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv](results/swarming_single_mutants_summary.csv) — one row per genotype: area, circularity and roundness means and SDs, ratios or differences versus wild type with 95% CIs, and Holm-adjusted p-values.
- [results/swarming_system_contrast.csv](results/swarming_system_contrast.csv) — rhl mutants versus las mutants for area, circularity and roundness.
- [results/swarming_single_mutants.png](results/swarming_single_mutants.png) — three-panel figure of area, circularity and roundness by genotype.

### To do

- [x] Explore the swarming data and check distributions
- [x] Write and run the R analysis
- [x] Write figure and numeric table to results/

## Co-culture rescue: does mixing ΔrhlI and ΔlasI restore swarming, and at which ratio?
<!-- rho:session c-67f77cfebaba2cea -->

### Question

When ΔrhlI and ΔlasI are grown together, does swarming recover to wild-type levels, and
does the recovery depend on the mixing ratio? I want the ratio at which colony area peaks,
how far the peak is from wild type and from the poorly swarming extremes, and how much of
the variation across ratios the ratio itself explains.

### Data & method

- [data/swarming/cocultures.csv](data/swarming/cocultures.csv) — one dish per row: alone cultures (wild type, ΔlasI, ΔrhlI) and ΔrhlI:ΔlasI mixes at twelve ratios from 1:3 to 1000:1, three dishes each, with `area`, `circularity` and `roundness`.
- [analysis/swarming_cocultures.R](analysis/swarming_cocultures.R) — reads the CSV, compares each mix ratio with wild type (Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity, Holm across the twelve ratios), fits a quadratic in log2(ratio) over the rescue window with a cluster bootstrap CI, a one-way ANOVA across the ten window ratios, a peak-to-wild-type bootstrap that resamples both mix and wild-type dishes, and sensitivity fits.

### Key results

- Alone, both mutants swarmed poorly: against a wild-type geometric mean area of 108,686, ΔrhlI was 10,263 (0.094×) and ΔlasI 14,522 (0.134×). See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- Grown together, the mutants recovered wild-type swarming: the fitted peak area was about 14× the ΔrhlI-alone and 10× the ΔlasI-alone geometric mean. The fitted peak was at 12.3:1 ΔrhlI:ΔlasI (cluster bootstrap 95% CI 10.4–14.7:1) with a fitted area of 145,880 (132,127–161,011), 1.34× wild type (bootstrap 95% CI 0.99–1.71). The nearest observed mix (10:1) was 1.64× wild type (0.83–3.25, unadjusted Welch p = 0.11; Holm 0.90), so the peak is statistically indistinguishable from wild type. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
- The ratio effect was strong and unimodal. Across the ten well-sampled ratios (1:3–100:1), ratio explained 93% of the variance in log area (one-way ANOVA F(9,20) = 29.5, p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹); the quadratic fit had R² = 0.891 versus 0.364 for a linear fit, its quadratic term was p = 7.7 × 10⁻¹², and a cubic term added nothing (p = 0.24). The fitted peak was 8.7× the 1:3 value, 2.1× the 100:1 value and 14.5× the 500:1 value; fitted area reached wild-type level between 3.2:1 and 46.4:1. Residual diagnostics were acceptable (Levene p = 0.94 on log area across the ten ratios, Shapiro–Wilk p = 0.67, largest Cook's D = 0.18). See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
- The low-ratio side was weakened but not resolved pairwise: 1:3, 1:2 and 1:1 mixes were 0.17× (95% CI 0.09–0.34), 0.25× (0.13–0.46) and 0.39× (0.21–0.72) wild type, but after Holm correction across the twelve ratios their p-values were 0.073, 0.078 and 0.121. The overall ratio test, not the pairwise tests, carries this part of the conclusion. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- The high-ratio side ended in a cliff. At 500:1 all three dishes failed (0.09× wild type, 95% CI 0.05–0.18, Holm p = 0.037 — the only mix significantly below wild type) and the colonies matched ΔrhlI alone; 1000:1 was heterogeneous (0.34× wild type, 95% CI 0.06–2.14; one dish near failure, two partially rescued). These two ratios were outside the fitted window. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
- Shape agreed on the same optimum: circularity reached its minimum at 12.2:1 (fitted 0.050 versus wild type 0.061), with the 10:1 mix at 0.69× wild type (0.39–1.22, Holm p = 0.87), while 1:3, 1:2 and 500:1 were 6.4–13.6× wild type (Holm p ≤ 0.017). Roundness peaked at 12.2:1 (0.97 versus wild type 0.855), so peak colonies were large and irregular in perimeter but not elongated. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).

![Colony area, circularity and roundness across ΔrhlI:ΔlasI mix ratios](results/swarming_cocultures.png)

### Choices

- Chose a quadratic in log2(ratio) over the 1:3–100:1 rescue window as the primary peak model. It gives a peak at 12.3:1 (95% CI 10.4–14.7), R² = 0.891, and leave-one-ratio-out peaks of 11.6–13.1, so the location is stable within the window. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
  - Alternative: including all twelve ratios gives a peak at 15.6:1 but the quadratic R² falls to 0.66 because the collapse at 500:1 is not quadratic; excluding only 500:1 shifts the peak to 22.4:1 (R² 0.75), and excluding only 1000:1 gives 11.2:1 (R² 0.93). The 1:3–100:1 window is the range where the smooth response is actually observed.
- Chose Welch t-tests on log area and log circularity for each mix ratio versus wild type, with Holm correction across the twelve ratios, as a descriptive check. For area only the 500:1 difference survives correction, so the ratio effect in area is inferred from the overall model rather than the pairwise tests. See [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: without correction the low ratios would be nominally significant (1:3 p = 0.0066, 1:2 p = 0.0078, 1:1 p = 0.013); the optimum and its CI do not depend on this choice, but the pairwise claim for the low-ratio decline would be stronger.
- Chose circularity as the primary shape readout and roundness as secondary. Both extrema fall at 12.2:1, so the peak location does not depend on the shape metric, but the interpretation does: circularity returns to wild-type level at the peak while roundness overshoots it. See [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv).
  - Alternative: treating roundness as primary would suggest the peak colonies have "better than wild-type" shape; the area and circularity results support large, irregular colonies rather than a shape improvement.

### Files

- [analysis/swarming_cocultures.R](analysis/swarming_cocultures.R) — the analysis: data reading, Welch comparisons, quadratic model, bootstraps, sensitivity fits, assumption checks and the figure; writes the three result files.
- [results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_summary.csv) — one row per condition (wild type, ΔlasI, ΔrhlI and the twelve mixes): n, area/circularity/roundness means and SDs, ratios or differences versus wild type with 95% CIs, and Holm-adjusted p-values.
- [results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv](results/swarming_cocultures_ratio_model.csv) — model fit, peak ratio and peak area with CIs, peak/wild-type ratio, fold changes, wild-type-level crossings, ratio R² and ANOVA p, sensitivity fits, assumption checks, and circularity/roundness extrema.
- [results/swarming_cocultures.png](results/swarming_cocultures.png) — three-panel figure: area with the fitted curve and peak, circularity with its fitted curve, and roundness points; wild-type and single-mutant reference lines.

### To do

- [x] Check the co-culture data and the existing analysis script
- [x] Run the analysis and validate the peak and ratio-effect estimates
- [x] Write the figure and numeric table to results/
- [x] Update the notes with the findings

## RNA-seq: what the quorum-sensing mutants change in gene expression
<!-- rho:session c-fa24dfd80dfe4bcb -->

### Question

For each medium (MMGluFeMinus, MMGluFePlus, Succinate), what changes in gene expression
when each mutant is compared with wild type: 97 (ΔrhlI), 98 (ΔlasI) and 99 (ΔlasIΔrhlI)?
How many genes change, which changes are strongest, and do the two single mutants change
the same genes?

### Data & method

- [data/rnaseq/counts.csv](data/rnaseq/counts.csv) — raw RNA-seq counts, one row per gene (5,828 genes) and one column per sample (36).
- [data/rnaseq/samples.csv](data/rnaseq/samples.csv) — the sample sheet: 3 media × 4 strains (1 wild type, 97, 98, 99) × 3 replicates, balanced.
- [data/rnaseq/annotation.csv](data/rnaseq/annotation.csv) — locus tag to gene name and product, used to label the strongest changes.
- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — DESeq2 analysis: one model with medium, strain and their interaction across all 36 samples, the nine mutant-vs-wild-type contrasts extracted per medium, shrunken log2 fold changes, FDR control and the overlap analysis between the single mutants; also draws the figure.

### Key results

- Nine contrasts, 5,828 genes tested in each. With FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1, the genes changed (up/down) were: in MMGluFeMinus 389 (209/180) for ΔrhlI, 384 (117/267) for ΔlasI and 1,362 (684/678) for ΔlasIΔrhlI; in MMGluFePlus 533 (187/346), 461 (135/326) and 1,345 (549/796); in Succinate 416 (38/378), 1,087 (371/716) and 1,166 (386/780). Counting FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast, three to four times more, so the two-fold set is the conservative one used here. See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
- The mutations themselves are visible in the counts. `lasI` was the strongest signal in the double mutant in every medium (−6.3 to −6.8; padj 8.2e-205 to 1.1e-230) and in ΔlasI in Succinate (−6.2; padj 7.5e-199); in the other two media it was still among the top five (−4.4 in MMGluFeMinus, −5.3 in MMGluFePlus; padj 6.0e-114 and 3.1e-162). `rhlI` fell in ΔrhlI (−2.3, −2.2, −1.6; padj 1.3e-4 to 6.5e-3) and further in the double mutant (−6.1 to −7.1). `rhlR` fell −2.7 to −4.4 and `lasR` −1.9 to −2.4 in the double mutant. See [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) and [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).
- Outside the quorum-sensing genes the strongest changes were medium-specific. Phenazine biosynthesis genes fell hard in ΔrhlI (`phzG2` −5.4 in MMGluFeMinus; `phzC1`/`phzB1`/`phzF1` −6.3 to −6.7 in Succinate) and in the double mutant (`phzC2` −9.1, `phzB2` −8.8 in MMGluFePlus; `phzB1` −8.9 in Succinate). Denitrification genes `norB`/`norC`/`norD` fell −3.8 to −4.0 in ΔrhlI and −5.3 to −6.4 in ΔlasI in MMGluFeMinus. In MMGluFePlus both single mutants lost oxidative-stress genes (`katB` −8.2 and −5.9; `trxB2`, `ahpF`, `ahpC`), and in Succinate ΔlasI lost `lasI`, `chiC`, `pa1L` and `cpbD`. The double mutant pushed these further (`rhlA` −8.1 in MMGluFeMinus, where ΔrhlI alone was −3.8; `lasA` −7.7 in Succinate, where ΔlasI alone was −2.6). See [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv).
- Where the two single mutants overlapped they mostly changed the same programme: 78 shared genes in MMGluFeMinus included the denitrification cluster `norB`/`norC`/`norD`/`nirS`/`nirM`/`nosZ`/`nosR`; 214 in MMGluFePlus included `katB`, `ahpF`, `trxB2` and `PA14_22320`/`PA14_53300`; 315 in Succinate included `phzA2`/`phzB2`/`phzG2`/`phzC2`, `chiC`, `cpbD` and `pa1L`. Direction agreed in 62/78 (79%), 209/214 (98%) and 313/315 (99%) of the shared genes; the MMGluFeMinus exceptions were `PA14_13370`/`PA14_13380`, up in ΔrhlI but strongly down in ΔlasI. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The overlap is far beyond chance in every medium (hypergeometric p 2.1e-20, 1.4e-112 and 1.5e-156; Jaccard 0.112, 0.274 and 0.265), but its size depends on the medium: about 20% of each mutant's changed genes were shared in MMGluFeMinus, 40–46% in MMGluFePlus, and in Succinate 76% of ΔrhlI's 416 changes were shared while only 29% of ΔlasI's 1,087 were. The genome-wide log2 fold-change correlation was 0.30, 0.53 and 0.66. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The double mutant changed more genes than either single (1,362/1,345/1,166), including 793/674/213 genes changed in neither single and 75/200/300 shared with both. Its fold changes were largely the sum of the two single effects: regressing the double mutant's log2FC on the sum of the single-mutant log2FCs gave slopes 1.04, 0.84 and 0.71 with R² 0.73, 0.73 and 0.90 (correlations 0.86, 0.85 and 0.95). Double-specific genes included `lecB` −5.7, `rhlR` −4.4, `aprA` −4.0 and `hsiB2`/`hsiF2` in MMGluFeMinus. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
- The largest single-mutant response was ΔlasI in Succinate (1,087 genes, 716 down), more than twice ΔrhlI in the same medium (416, 378 down); ΔrhlI in MMGluFePlus was also mostly down (346 of 533). ΔlasI's Succinate-specific set included `lasI` itself and the non-ribosomal peptide synthetase cluster `PA14_34810`/`PA14_34820`/`PA14_34830`/`PA14_34840`, while the double mutant's Succinate response was close to the union of the two singles (1,166 versus 1,188 genes). See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
- The strain identities hold in the counts: `lasI` is near-absent in 98 and 99, and `rhlI` is strongly reduced in 97 (about 22% of wild type in MMGluFeMinus) and near-absent in 99. Five genes carry one Cook's-distance outlier each and are flagged rather than removed, among them `rhlI` and `lasB`. See [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).

![Genes changed per mutant and medium, overlap of the two single mutants, fold-change agreement and a heatmap of the strongest genes](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png)

### Choices

- Chose one saturated DESeq2 model over all 36 samples (design `~ Group`, twelve medium × strain groups, local dispersion trend) and extracted the nine within-medium contrasts. It shares dispersion information across groups. See [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv).
  - Alternative: three independent per-medium fits (12 samples each, design `~ Strain`) give the same log2FCs (correlation 1.000) and Jaccard overlap 0.83–0.96 with the primary changed sets; counts differ by at most 58 genes (e.g. 533 versus 560 for ΔrhlI in MMGluFePlus).
- Chose FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 as the definition of a changed gene, reporting both the two-fold and FDR-only counts. See [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv).
  - Alternative: FDR alone gives 1,299–3,585 genes per contrast instead of 384–1,362; the ordering of mutants and media does not change, but many small, statistically supported shifts would be counted as changes.
- Chose to keep all genes and flag Cook's-distance outliers rather than let DESeq2 remove them. With three replicates the default filter removes five genes from every contrast entirely, including `rhlI` and `lasB`, because one replicate of each is an outlier; the counts change by at most five genes and the log2FC correlation is 1.000. See [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) and the `cooks_outlier` column of [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv).
  - Alternative: the default Cook's filter gives 387 versus 389 changed genes for ΔrhlI in MMGluFeMinus, and 1,358 versus 1,362 for the double mutant, with Jaccard 0.993–0.998 against the primary sets.
- Chose normal-prior log2 fold-change shrinkage (from DESeq2) because `apeglm` and `ashr` are not installed; significance uses the unshrunken fold changes, and both values are in the table. The top genes by adjusted p-value are unaffected by this choice.
- Chose the hypergeometric test on the 5,828-gene universe to test whether the single-mutant overlap exceeds chance, and report Jaccard and direction agreement alongside it because the test alone does not show how much of each mutant's response is shared. See [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv).
  - Alternative: reporting only the Jaccard index or only the overlap counts gives the same ordering across media (MMGluFeMinus lowest, Succinate/MMGluFePlus higher) but hides the strong asymmetry between ΔrhlI and ΔlasI in Succinate.

### Files

- [results/summary.md](results/summary.md) — the project's three questions and answers, with key numbers and figures; the short entry point to the detailed result files.
- [results/summary.png](results/summary.png) — one-page, three-panel summary figure: mutant areas vs wild type, the co-culture ratio response with its fitted peak, and genes changed per mutant and medium.
- [analysis/summary_figure.R](analysis/summary_figure.R) — reads the existing result tables and draws results/summary.png; no models are refitted.
- [analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R](analysis/rnaseq_differential_expression.R) — the analysis: annotation parsing, DESeq2 model, nine contrasts, overlap and additivity analysis, sensitivity fits, top-gene table and four-panel figure.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.csv) — compact differential-expression table: 7,143 rows, only the calls passing FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1 in each contrast, with 15 columns (comparison, medium, strain, mutant, locus, gene, product, baseMean, raw and shrunken log2FC, standard error, p-value, adjusted p-value, direction and Cook's-outlier flag). The full 52,452-row table was removed to keep the project small.
- [results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv](results/rnaseq_de_summary.csv) — one row per contrast: genes tested, changed at FDR < 0.05, changed at FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| ≥ 1, up, down and outlier-flagged genes.
- [results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv](results/rnaseq_mutant_overlap.csv) — one row per medium: counts changed in 97, 98 and 99, overlap and Jaccard, direction agreement, hypergeometric p, log2FC correlations, double-mutant sharing and additivity fit.
- [results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv](results/rnaseq_sensitivity.csv) — one row per contrast: changed genes and agreement for the primary model, the per-medium fits and the default Cook's filter.
- [results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv](results/rnaseq_top_genes.csv) — the ten strongest genes per contrast by adjusted p-value and by |log2FC| (baseMean ≥ 100), with annotation.
- [results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png](results/rnaseq_differential_expression.png) — four-panel figure: changed genes per mutant and medium split by direction; overlap of the two single mutants; log2FC agreement between ΔrhlI and ΔlasI with the identity line; heatmap of the top six genes per contrast across all 36 samples.

### To do

- [x] Check the counts, sample sheet and annotation
- [x] Run the differential-expression models and inspect the results
- [x] Write the DE table and figure to results/
- [x] Fill in the findings and choices
- [x] Write results/summary.md with the project's three conclusions
- [x] Draw results/summary.png
